Ubisoft Logs Strong Bookings as Players Welcome Assassin's Creed Remake
By Mauro Orru

Ubisoft Entertainment reported robust net bookings for its fiscal second quarter as a remake of Assassin's Creed fared well, a boost for the videogame developer as it seeks to get its finances back on track following a major overhaul of its operations.

The French videogame group reported 388.9 million euros ($426.9 million) in net bookings for the three months to the end of September, down nearly 21% on year, but above company guidance of around 370 million euros. An on-year decline was widely expected as analysts had forecast net bookings of 350.7 million euros, according to Visible Alpha.

The company said that "Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced," a remake of 2013's "Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag" that Ubisoft released on July 9, had lifted bookings above guidance, while the rest of the Assassin's Creed catalog, the Ghost Recon franchise and "Invincible: Guarding the Globe" also fared well.

Better-than-expected bookings come as Ubisoft has been overhauling its operations in a bid to shore up its finances after a few difficult years in which the group issued several profit warnings. It has created five business units known as creative houses, each with its own leadership team focusing on specific types of games to reduce complexity and streamline decision-making.
Chief Executive Yves Guillemot said the success of "Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced" and renewed momentum of "Rainbow Six Siege" were among the first benefits of the new structure.

"In an increasingly competitive entertainment industry, gamers require exceptional quality, distinctive creative experiences, uncompromising gameplay and a defined audience for games to stand out and succeed," he said.

The company has discontinued and postponed several games, closed some studios and cut hundreds of jobs in an effort to turn its business around. On Thursday, it said it was reducing its workforce by another 166 positions across its Montreal and Quebec City operations.

Guillemot had warned in May that the fiscal year to the end of March 2027 would mark a low point in Ubisoft's free cash flow trajectory, along with a softer release slate of games and restructuring costs. However, he said Ubisoft would emerge with a stronger pipeline and better financials from fiscal 2028 onward. On Thursday, he said the group remained on track with its cost reduction program and had made progress on its refinancing plan.

Ubisoft reported a non-IFRS operating loss of 155.9 million euros for the first half of the fiscal year compared with a profit of 27.1 million euros a year earlier. Analysts had forecast an operating loss of 94.7 million euros, according to Visible Alpha. Its statutory net loss grew to 254.5 million euros from 161.3 million euros a year earlier.

For fiscal 2027, the company said it continued to expect net bookings to fall by a high single-digit percentage from the nearly 1.53 billion euros it reported for fiscal 2026. It also expects to post a high single-digit percentage negative non-IFRS operating margin.
